title: The Kiss by Gustav Klimt
description: Klimt’s gold-leaf painting of an embracing couple, made at the height of his “golden period”: why it looks the way it does and what it says about Vienna around 1900. It hangs in the Upper Belvedere.

title: The Hunters in the Snow by Pieter Bruegel the Elder
description: A winter scene from 1565 of hunters trudging home above a frozen valley, part of a series on the seasons. Explains how Bruegel built the view and what village life it records. In the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

title: The Garden of Earthly Delights by Hieronymus Bosch
description: Bosch’s three-panel altarpiece moving from Eden to a crowded garden of pleasure to a strange hell, panel by panel, with what its odd details may have meant around 1500. In the Prado.

title: Guernica by Pablo Picasso
description: Picasso’s huge black-and-white response to the 1937 bombing of a Basque town: how he made it in weeks, what the bull, horse and lamp might mean, and its long road to Madrid. At the Reina Sofía.

title: Las Meninas by Diego Velázquez
description: Velázquez paints himself at work beside the young Spanish princess and her attendants, with the king and queen glimpsed in a mirror. Unpicks who is looking at whom, and why. In the Prado.

title: The Black Paintings by Francisco Goya
description: The dark murals, Saturn among them, that an aging, deaf Goya painted on the walls of his own house, later moved to canvas. This part covers the paintings and what they suggest about his state of mind. In the Prado.

title: The Birth of Venus by Sandro Botticelli
description: Botticelli’s goddess arriving on a shell, painted for the Medici circle: the classical myth behind it, who may have posed, and why a pagan nude was a bold choice in 1480s Florence. In the Uffizi.

title: The School of Athens by Raphael
description: Raphael’s fresco of ancient philosophers gathered in an imagined hall, painted for the pope’s rooms: who is who, including the faces borrowed from Leonardo and Michelangelo. In the Raphael Rooms, Vatican.

title: Apollo and Daphne by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
description: Bernini’s marble of a nymph turning into a laurel tree as the god catches her, carved in his early twenties: how he made stone look like skin, leaves and motion. At the Galleria Borghese.

title: The Raft of the Medusa by Théodore Géricault
description: A huge painting of survivors of an 1816 French shipwreck, adrift on a raft: the scandal behind the disaster, and how Géricault studied corpses and survivors to paint it. In the Louvre.

title: Water Lilies by Claude Monet
description: Monet’s late paintings of the pond in his Giverny garden, made while his eyesight failed. The largest of them fill two oval rooms he designed with the state at the Musée de l’Orangerie.

title: The Thinker by Auguste Rodin
description: Rodin’s seated bronze man began as Dante at the top of his Gates of Hell. Explains how it became a standalone figure. The best-known large cast sits in the garden of the Musée Rodin.

title: Napoleon Crossing the Alps by Jacques-Louis David
description: David’s portrait of Napoleon on a rearing horse in an Alpine pass, a picture of a crossing that really happened on a mule. How it was made as propaganda, in five versions. The first is at Malmaison.

title: The Ambassadors by Hans Holbein the Younger
description: Holbein’s 1533 double portrait of two French envoys surrounded by instruments and books, with a distorted skull across the floor. Explains the objects and how to see the skull. In the National Gallery.

title: The Scream by Edvard Munch
description: Munch’s figure clutching its face under a blood-red sky above the Oslo fjord: the experience behind it and why he made several versions. The 1893 painting is in the National Museum; others are at the Munch Museum.

title: The Potato Eaters by Vincent van Gogh
description: Van Gogh’s dark early painting of a peasant family eating by lamplight, made in 1885 before he went to Paris: what he wanted it to say and why critics disliked it. In the Van Gogh Museum.

title: Tree Roots by Vincent van Gogh
description: The tangle of roots and trunks Van Gogh was likely working on the day he shot himself in 1890, and the recent discovery of the exact spot in Auvers he painted. In the Van Gogh Museum.

title: Las Meninas by Diego Velázquez
description: A short episode on the Spanish court painter’s puzzle of a picture: the princess, her maids, the painter at his easel and the king and queen in a mirror. Hangs in the Prado.

title: The Birth of Venus by Sandro Botticelli
description: Why a goddess arriving on a seashell became the picture of the Florentine Renaissance, and what the myth meant to the Medici circle. In the Uffizi.

title: Judith Slaying Holofernes by Artemisia Gentileschi
description: The biblical widow and her maid killing an enemy general, painted by a woman who had survived assault and a public trial. The episode reads the painting through her life. In the Uffizi.

title: The Night Watch by Rembrandt
description: Rembrandt’s huge group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company caught mid-movement, and how he used light to pull it out of the dark. Hangs in its own gallery at the Rijksmuseum.

title: Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci
description: Tamar Avishai goes to the Louvre to see Leonardo’s portrait through the crowds and asks why this one small painting became the most famous in the world.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck
description: A merchant couple in their room in Bruges, painted in fine detail down to the convex mirror on the back wall. The episode works through those details. In the National Gallery.

title: Guernica by Pablo Picasso
description: Melvyn Bragg and guests on the bombing of Guernica in 1937, how Picasso turned it into a huge black-and-white canvas, and the painting’s long road to the Reina Sofía.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Lewis Chessmen, walrus-ivory chess pieces
description: Neil MacGregor on the 12th-century chess pieces found on the Isle of Lewis: where they were probably carved in Norway, how chess travelled from India, and what the glum little figures say about medieval Europe.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Sutton Hoo Helmet, an Anglo-Saxon king’s helmet
description: Neil MacGregor on the iron-and-bronze helmet from a 7th-century ship burial in Suffolk, how it was rebuilt from hundreds of fragments, and what it shows about kings in early England.

title: Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear by Vincent van Gogh
description: A slow, guided look at the portrait Van Gogh painted weeks after cutting off part of his ear in Arles: the bandage, the Japanese print behind him, and what he wanted people to see.

title: Las Meninas by Diego Velázquez
description: A close look at Velázquez’s painting of the Spanish princess, her maids and the painter himself at work, and why the mirror at the back still has people arguing about who is being painted.

title: The Hunters in the Snow by Pieter Bruegel the Elder
description: Tired hunters come home over a frozen valley in Bruegel’s winter scene. The episode walks through the details, the cycle of seasons it belonged to, and how it came to Vienna.

title: The Night Watch by Rembrandt van Rijn
description: Rembrandt’s group portrait of an Amsterdam civic guard company: who paid for it, why it looks so busy compared with other militia pictures, and what happened when it was cut down to fit a wall.

title: Hermine Gallia by Gustav Klimt
description: Klimt’s full-length portrait of a wealthy Viennese woman in a white dress, painted just before his gold period, and how it ended up as one of very few Klimts in Britain.

title: Bathers at Asnières by Georges Seurat
description: Seurat’s big canvas of working men resting by the Seine near Paris, painted when he was 24, and how it was rejected by the official Salon before ending up in London.

title: The Skating Minister by Henry Raeburn
description: A Church of Scotland minister gliding across a frozen loch just outside Edinburgh, arms folded. Who he was, why the picture became a Scottish icon, and the doubts once raised over who painted it.

title: Seated Woman with Bent Knees by Egon Schiele
place: National Gallery Prague, Trade Fair Palace
description: Schiele’s 1917 picture of a woman sitting with her knees drawn up, looking straight out. The episode looks at how he drew bodies and why his work shocked Vienna. Held by the National Gallery Prague.

title: The Death of Marat by Jacques-Louis David
place: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
description: David’s painting of the murdered revolutionary journalist slumped in his bath, made within months of the killing in 1793. How it turned a political murder into something like a religious image. In Brussels.

title: Virgin and Child with Canon van der Paele by Jan van Eyck
description: An elderly canon kneels before the Virgin and Child with two saints, painted in close detail down to his wrinkles and spectacles. The episode works through the picture. In Bruges, a day trip from Brussels.

title: Amor Victorious by Caravaggio
description: Caravaggio’s grinning, half-grown Cupid stepping over the symbols of music, war and learning, painted for a Roman collector around 1602. Who modelled, and why it caused talk. In the Gemäldegalerie.

title: Whistler’s Mother by James McNeill Whistler
description: Whistler’s side-on portrait of his mother in black against a grey wall, which he called an arrangement in grey and black. How it was made and how it became an emblem far beyond art. In the Musée d’Orsay.

title: Starry Night over the Rhône by Vincent van Gogh
description: Van Gogh’s night view of the river at Arles, with gaslights reflected in the water and a couple on the bank, painted in 1888. Discussed with Van Gogh writer Martin Bailey. In the Musée d’Orsay.

title: Rain, Steam and Speed by J.M.W. Turner
description: Turner’s steam train charging over a Thames bridge through rain and mist in 1844. What railways meant then, the hare racing the engine, and how loose the paint really is. In the National Gallery.

title: The Fighting Temeraire by J.M.W. Turner
description: An old warship from Trafalgar towed up the Thames by a small steam tug to be broken up, under a blazing sunset. The episode explains the story and what Turner changed. In the National Gallery.

title: The Ambassadors by Hans Holbein the Younger
description: Two French envoys in London in 1533, with a shelf of instruments between them and a stretched skull across the floor. What the objects mean and where to stand to see the skull. In the National Gallery.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck
description: A merchant and his wife in their room in Bruges in 1434, with a small round mirror on the back wall showing two more people. Who they were and what the details may mean. In the National Gallery.

title: Ruby Loftus Screwing a Breech-ring by Laura Knight
description: A young factory worker machining part of an anti-aircraft gun in 1943, painted by Laura Knight for the government’s war artists scheme. Who Ruby Loftus was and what the picture was for.

title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows by John Constable
description: Constable’s storm over Salisbury Cathedral with a rainbow breaking through, painted after his wife’s death. What troubled him at the time and what the weather is doing in the picture. Owned by Tate.

title: The Calling of Saint Matthew by Caravaggio
description: Christ points across a dim room at a tax collector counting money at a table, in light that falls like a beam. Which figure is Matthew, and how the scene fits its chapel. Still in the church it was painted for.

title: The Conversion of Saint Paul by Caravaggio
description: Saul thrown from his horse on the road to Damascus, lying on his back in a burst of light while the horse fills the frame. The episode looks at the story and how Caravaggio staged it.

title: Augustus of Prima Porta, Roman marble statue
description: A marble statue of Rome’s first emperor, found at his wife’s villa in 1863, posed as a commander with a carved breastplate full of political messages. How to read it. In the Vatican Museums.

title: The Deposition by Jacopo Pontormo
description: Pontormo’s altarpiece of Christ’s body being carried, in pinks and pale blues, with figures that seem to float. Why it looks so strange for the 1520s. Still in its chapel in the church of Santa Felicita.

title: The Haywain Triptych by Hieronymus Bosch
description: Bosch’s three-panel altarpiece with a huge cart of hay at its centre, everyone from peasants to the pope grabbing at it, between Eden and hell. What the hay stands for. In the Prado.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Mummy of Hornedjitef, an Egyptian priest’s coffin and body
description: The first episode: Neil MacGregor on the mummy and painted coffins of a Theban priest from around 240 BC, and what they tell us about Egyptian beliefs about the afterlife.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Olduvai Handaxe, a stone tool
description: A 1.2-million-year-old stone axe from Tanzania’s Olduvai Gorge, and how this all-purpose tool shows early humans planning, sharing skills and starting to spread out of Africa.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Swimming Reindeer, an Ice Age carving
description: Two reindeer carved from a mammoth tusk about 13,000 years ago in France, and what they say about the first art and the minds of Ice Age hunters.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Ain Sakhri Lovers, a stone figurine
description: A small calcite pebble carved about 11,000 years ago near Bethlehem showing a couple embracing, possibly the oldest image of people making love, and what it says about early farming life.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Jade Axe, a Neolithic ceremonial axe
description: A polished jade axe head found in Kent but quarried high in the Italian Alps 6,000 years ago, and why people carried such a useless, beautiful thing across Europe.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Flood Tablet, a cuneiform clay tablet
description: A clay tablet from Nineveh telling of a great flood long before the Bible’s, how a self-taught scholar decoded it in 1872, and what it says about the world’s oldest stories.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus
description: An Egyptian scroll of maths problems from about 1550 BC, covering fractions, bread rations and pyramid slopes, and what it shows about how ancient Egypt was run.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Minoan Bull-leaper, a bronze figure
description: A small bronze from Crete of an acrobat somersaulting over a charging bull, and how the Minoans, and later Victorian archaeologists, shaped our idea of early Greece.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Mold Gold Cape, a Bronze Age cape
description: A cape beaten from a single gold ingot about 3,700 years ago, found in a Welsh burial mound in 1833, and what it says about wealth and power in Bronze Age Britain.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Statue of Ramesses II
description: The huge granite bust of Egypt’s best-known pharaoh, how it was dragged to London in 1818, and how Ramesses used statues like this to project power.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Lachish Reliefs, Assyrian palace carvings
description: Stone panels from Sennacherib’s palace at Nineveh showing the siege of the Judean city of Lachish in 701 BC, an early piece of war reporting made for a king.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Gold Coin of Croesus
description: A small gold coin from Lydia in modern Turkey, minted around 550 BC by the famously rich King Croesus, and how pure-metal coins changed trade.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Oxus Chariot Model, a Persian gold model
description: A tiny gold chariot from the Oxus Treasure, made in the Persian Empire around 500 BC, and what it tells us about how that vast empire was held together by roads.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Rosetta Stone
description: Neil MacGregor on the stone slab with one decree in three scripts, how it unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs, and why a tax decree became the museum’s most visited object.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Head of Augustus, a bronze Roman portrait
description: A bronze head of Rome’s first emperor, cut from a statue and buried under a temple step in Meroë, Sudan, by raiders who wanted it trodden on, and what it says about Roman propaganda.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Warren Cup, a Roman silver cup
description: A Roman silver drinking cup decorated with scenes of male lovers, why it shocked collectors for decades, and what it says about sex and status in the Roman world.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Hoxne Pepper Pot, a Roman silver pot
description: A silver pepper pot shaped like a Roman lady, from a hoard buried in Suffolk around AD 400, and how pepper from India reached the edge of the empire.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Hinton St Mary Mosaic, a Roman floor
description: A 4th-century floor mosaic from a Dorset villa with one of the earliest known pictures of Christ, and how Christianity and pagan myth sat side by side in Roman Britain.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Statue of Tara, a Buddhist bronze
description: A gilded bronze of the Buddhist goddess Tara from Sri Lanka, about 1,200 years old, and how statues like this spread Buddhism across Asia.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Ife Head, a brass portrait
description: A brass head made in the West African city of Ife around 1400, why its realism stunned Europeans in the 1930s, and what it says about a powerful kingdom.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Hoa Hakananai’a, an Easter Island statue
description: A basalt figure taken from Rapa Nui in 1868, the carvings on its back added when the island’s religion changed, and the island’s calls for its return.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Taíno Ritual Seat, a carved wooden seat
description: A carved wooden seat made by the Taíno of the Caribbean, used by leaders to speak with spirits, and what happened to the Taíno after Columbus arrived.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: Dürer’s Rhinoceros by Albrecht Dürer
description: The 1515 woodcut of a rhino Dürer never saw, drawn from a sketch and a letter, and how this wrong picture fixed what Europeans thought a rhino looked like for centuries.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Mechanical Galleon, a clockwork table ornament
description: A gilded clockwork ship made in Augsburg around 1585 that rolled down banquet tables, fired cannons and played music, and what it says about power and technology in Renaissance Europe.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Benin Plaque: The Oba with Europeans, a brass plaque
description: A 16th-century brass plaque from the royal palace of Benin showing the king with Portuguese traders, and how it came to London after the British looted the city in 1897.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Akan Drum, a West African drum
description: A drum made by the Akan people of West Africa, taken to Virginia on a slave ship and later collected in America, and what it carries of the history of the Atlantic slave trade.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Great Wave by Katsushika Hokusai
description: Hokusai’s print of a huge wave and Mount Fuji, made around 1831 as Japan was closed to the world, and what its Prussian blue ink and Western perspective say about change coming.

channel: A History of the World in 100 Objects
title: The Throne of Weapons, a sculpture from decommissioned guns
description: A chair made in Mozambique in 2001 from guns handed in after the civil war, and what it says about turning weapons into art after decades of fighting.

title: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump by Joseph Wright of Derby
description: A slow, guided look at Wright’s candlelit scene of a travelling scientist pumping the air from a glass bowl with a bird inside, and the faces of the family watching it.

title: The Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci
description: The longer cut of the channel’s Mona Lisa video: who the sitter was, how Leonardo built up the soft haze on her face over years, and how a 1911 theft made the portrait famous. In the Louvre.

title: David by Michelangelo
description: The marble giant Michelangelo carved in his twenties from a block others had given up on: how he did it, why the proportions look odd up close, and what the figure meant to the Florentine Republic. In the Accademia.

title: The Milkmaid by Johannes Vermeer
description: Vermeer’s small painting of a kitchen maid pouring milk: how he made light, bread and plaster wall look so real, and why a plain household task was worth painting in 1650s Delft. In the Rijksmuseum.

title: The Taking of Christ by Caravaggio
description: Caravaggio’s night scene of Judas kissing Christ as soldiers close in, and the story of how the lost painting turned up in 1990 in a Jesuit house in Dublin. In the National Gallery of Ireland.

title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère by Édouard Manet
description: Manet’s last big painting: a barmaid at a Paris music hall, with a mirror behind her that doesn’t quite add up. A long, unhurried look at why. It hangs in the Courtauld Gallery at Somerset House.

title: Seaport with the Embarkation of the Queen of Sheba by Claude Lorrain
description: A golden sunrise over an imagined harbour, painted in Rome in 1648. Turner loved it so much he asked to hang beside it, and he still does, in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Sagrada Família by Antoni Gaudí
description: Gaudí’s basilica, begun in 1882 and still being built. The episode looks at how one building became a lifelong obsession, and what to look for in its stone forest of columns.

title: Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci
description: The world’s most famous portrait, taken slowly: who she was, how Leonardo painted that smile, and how a theft in 1911 made her a celebrity. She hangs in the Louvre’s largest room.

title: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump by Joseph Wright of Derby
description: A travelling scientist pumps the air out of a glass bowl while a family watches a bird struggle, lit by one candle. A scene from the Age of Enlightenment, at the National Gallery.

title: Self-Portrait as Saint Catherine of Alexandria by Artemisia Gentileschi
description: Artemisia painted herself as a martyred saint, holding the broken wheel she was tortured on. The National Gallery bought it in 2018, its first painting by her.

title: Miss La La at the Cirque Fernando by Edgar Degas
description: An acrobat hangs from a rope by her teeth, high under a circus dome in 1879 Paris. Degas painted her from below, as the crowd saw her. At the National Gallery.

title: The Great Piece of Turf by Albrecht Dürer
description: A watercolour of grasses and dandelions from 1503, studied as closely as any portrait. It belongs to the Albertina. Being on paper, it’s only shown now and then, so check before you go.

title: The Courtyard of a House in Delft by Pieter de Hooch
description: A quiet Dutch courtyard in 1658: brick paths, a maid, a child, a doorway into the street. A small painting about ordinary life, at the National Gallery.

title: The Jewish Bride by Rembrandt
description: A couple in an embrace, his hand on her heart, painted thickly in gold and red late in Rembrandt’s life. Van Gogh said he’d give ten years to sit in front of it. In the Rijksmuseum.

title: Going to the Match by L.S. Lowry
description: Crowds of Lowry’s “matchstick men” stream toward Bolton Wanderers’ old ground. Owned by the footballers’ union and shown at The Lowry arts centre in Salford.

title: The Triumphs of Caesar by Andrea Mantegna
description: Nine huge canvases of a Roman victory parade, painted for the Gonzaga court in Mantua and bought by Charles I. They hang in their own gallery at Hampton Court Palace.

title: Portrait of Pope Innocent X by Diego Velázquez
description: Velázquez’s portrait of a sharp-eyed pope in red silk, from 1650. The pope reportedly called it “too true”. It’s still owned by his family, in their palace gallery on Via del Corso.

title: The Alexander Mosaic, from Pompeii’s House of the Faun
description: A floor of about a million tiny stones showing Alexander the Great charging the Persian king Darius. Found in Pompeii in 1831, now in Naples’ archaeological museum.

title: The Snail by Henri Matisse
description: Too ill to paint, Matisse cut shapes from painted paper and had them pinned into a spiral. One of his last big works, from 1953, at Tate Modern.

title: Portrait of the Journalist Sylvia von Harden by Otto Dix
description: A monocled writer with a cigarette and a cocktail in 1926 Berlin, painted with cool cruelty. It came to stand for the Weimar era’s new woman. In the Centre Pompidou.

title: The Descent from the Cross by Peter Paul Rubens
description: Rubens’s huge altarpiece of Christ’s body being lowered from the cross, made for Antwerp’s cathedral in 1612 and still there. Antwerp is about 45 minutes from Brussels by train.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck
description: A Bruges merchant and his wife in 1434, with a mirror on the back wall that reflects two more people. Who are they, and what is going on? At the National Gallery.

title: Jupiter and Io by Correggio
description: The god Jupiter, disguised as a dark cloud, embraces the nymph Io. A soft, strange painting from the 1530s, in the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

title: The Garden of Earthly Delights by Hieronymus Bosch
description: Bosch’s three-panel vision of paradise, earthly pleasure and hell, crowded with strange creatures. A short tour of its meaning, at the Prado.

title: The Cradle by Berthe Morisot
description: Morisot’s sister watches over her sleeping baby through a gauze veil. It hung in the first Impressionist show in 1874. In the Musée d’Orsay.

title: Potsdamer Platz by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner
description: Two streetwalkers on a traffic island in Berlin’s busiest square in 1914, painted in jagged, sickly colours. In the Neue Nationalgalerie, a few minutes from the real square.

title: A Bigger Splash by David Hockney
description: A California swimming pool, an empty chair and the splash of someone who just dived in, from 1967. In the Tate collection, usually on show at Tate Britain.

title: Bal du moulin de la Galette by Pierre-Auguste Renoir
description: A Sunday dance in Montmartre, 1876, with sunlight falling through the trees onto the crowd. In the Musée d’Orsay.

title: Yellow-Red-Blue by Wassily Kandinsky
description: Kandinsky believed colours could sound like music. This 1925 painting is one of his attempts to show it. In the Centre Pompidou’s modern art museum.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck
description: Why a small 1434 double portrait of a Bruges merchant and his wife is so full of riddles, from the mirror to the little dog. At the National Gallery.

title: The Seagram Murals by Mark Rothko
description: Dark red and maroon paintings made for a New York restaurant, which Rothko refused to hand over. He gave nine to the Tate, where they fill their own room at Tate Modern.
